builder_plan.scenario: Your coding assistant makes changes that still need substantial repair before merging.
builder_plan.change: Try the technique on held-out issues from a repository with reliable tests.
builder_plan.baseline: The same coding agent, repository snapshot, tools, and token budget.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Correct patches, regression failures, human repair time, and total cost per accepted change.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Testing with Coding Agents: A Large-Scale Comparison of Agent-Supported and Human-Authored Pull Requests
summary: This paper proposes no deployable technique; it is a large-scale empirical study (114,134 PRs in 391 Java repositories) comparing testing behavior in agent-supported versus human-authored pull requests, so it replaces nothing in the production stack. Adoption costs nothing directly, but acting on its findings would require adding PR-level telemetry and review checks for agent-generated tests, which consumes team time. What can fail is over-interpreting the results: pooled cross-project comparisons reverse or hide within-repository effects, test-quality differences (smells, coverage) are borderline or absent, and the analysis is limited to Java repositories with five detected agents, so conclusions may not transfer to other languages or tools.
rationale: The study offers useful governance signals (agent-supported PRs add tests more often but modify and delete them less, with uncertain quality effects) but provides no adoptable method and no quantified performance gain, so the reader should monitor this evidence rather than change production practice.
technique: Empirical comparison of agent-authored vs human test PRs
